utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning technicians and good morning interpreters. I also say good morning to the public in the gallery which represents the international community. And today the case before us will be what, Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be case number IT-95-14/1, the Prosecutor versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Will the Prosecution please introduce itself for the record. Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, my name is Niemann, and I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Meddegoda and Ms. Erasmus, for the Prosecution, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And for the Defence, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Goran Mikulicic with Mr. Joka. I am appearing for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We shall then continue with the testimony. Good morning, witness. You will recall that yesterday you made a solemn declaration to speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Are you in the same spirit today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Percinlic, I am wondering if I could just ask you some questions to start off with about your processes through becoming a judge and so forth. I think you told us yesterday that originally you studied law at Banja Luka, and soon after that you were appointed as a judge?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you were initially appointed, when was that, the date, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: 1987. Before that I was a professional associate and for a short while I worked for a company.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you were appointed in 1987. Who appointed you? Can you tell us the processes of how you become appointed in 1987?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: The procedure was as follows: At that time it was called the basic court for three municipalities, Travnik, Vitez and Novi Travnik. I was appointed by the three municipal councils.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So were those courts at that stage within the administration of the three municipalities? Is that how it worked, or was there a link or a reference to the republican government in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: There was a link with the republican government of Sarajevo, because administratively and organisationally speaking they were under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. Now, was there then any link from there to the federal government in Belgrade, or did it end at the republican level?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: It ended at the republican level at that time. I mean, as far as the courts are concerned. The federation had its own courts or, rather, the federal court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the jurisdiction that you had in the three municipalities, was that just a general criminal law jurisdiction or a combination of criminal and civil law, in terms of property disputes and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Our jurisdiction was related to the civil law and the criminal law, up to a certain level, up to a certain degree of punishment for a particular crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the appellate process, it went from your court that you were appointed to in 1987, did it go directly to the supreme court, or was there an intermediate appellate court?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: It did not go directly to the supreme court. There was an intermediate court, appellate court in Zenica, and that was the higher court in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And it was called the higher court, was it, the higher court of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And from there you could appeal to the supreme court, no doubt on limited circumstances, but you could then get from there to the supreme court in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, but only in some cases. Only -- specific legal situations -- it would take a very long time to explain all the proceedings and procedures, but one usually went to the second instance court in Zenica, and in certain cases to the supreme court in Sarajevo, and the civil law and the appeals were filed with the higher court in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I don't want to trouble you with all the fine details of the appellate procedure. I am just trying to establish the structure. Now, did the supreme court of Sarajevo, did it sit in regional centres at all, or did it stay seated in Sarajevo? And I am speaking of the period leading up to 1991, say.

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Until 1991, it had its permanent seat in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did it occasionally move to other centres, or did it only ever sit in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they always sat in Sarajevo, that is, until April, 1991 or, rather, until April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you were then -- when were you next appointed? When were you appointed to the district military court in Travnik? When did that take place, your actual appointment there?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: On the 22nd December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, who appointed you to the district military court in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: The presidency of the Croat community of Herceg-Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where was that government or that presidency? Where was that located?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: In Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what happened to your old position, the old position you had as a judge? Did that continue on and someone else was appointed to it, or was it dissolved?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you came to be appointed to the district military court in Travnik, was there a law introduced to create a new judicial structure? Can you give us some more explanation as to how it came about that it was established and how it was structured?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: First, a decree was passed, and I think it was in November, 1992, establishing the organisational layout, organisational structure, and competencies and everything else that was needed for the work of military courts. And yesterday I explained why it was necessary to set up such courts under those extraordinary circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the district military court in Travnik having under it several municipalities, I think you said eight or ten. Can you remember the municipalities that came under the jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us those municipalities? I have a map here, if that would help you.

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, it was quite a long time ago, so I am not sure I remember them all, but I can mention several municipalities, those were Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf, Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak, Kresevo, Fojnica, and I believe Zavidovici. It's difficult to see the decree. It's a long time since I saw those documents, because it has been not in force. It has not been applied for the past three or perhaps more than three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what about -- I think you mentioned Vitez. What about Zenica? Did it come under the jurisdiction of your court?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: You see, the jurisdiction of these courts, I explained yesterday, they were the courts of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council. But the jurisdiction could not be differentiated territorially, because the municipalities are mixed. So that there were some HVO forces in Zenica as well, and they were under us too, or rather, we conducted court proceedings against persons who were members of these formations. And now I remember also members of the Croat Defence Council in Zepce. That is, jurisdiction could not be divided, defined strictly territorially, because the military court, with a seat in Travnik, that is the court of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, had its jurisdiction over the formations of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which were quartered in Vitez or in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had the equivalent or similar district military court as did the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the -- I think you said yesterday that there was an appeal from your court to the supreme court, that's the supreme court of Sarajevo -- sorry, the supreme court of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No. During that period of time it was not possible to file an appeal or submit a case to the supreme court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because of the well-known fact that Sarajevo was completely closed and, for that reason, as far as I can remember, sometime in '92 a decree was passed, I do not know who it was that passed it, whereby the departments of the supreme court in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina were established. And such a department, as far as I know, existed both in Zenica and in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And is it correct that the appeal, that an appeal from the district military court of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the supreme court of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zenica, and that the appeals from your court went to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I wanted to ask you some questions, if I could, about the legal foundation for these courts. The courts of the HVO, what was the foundation, legally, of the HVO in Bosnia-Herzegovina, say, in November of 1992? What did you rely on as the constitutional foundation? And if you have difficulty understanding the question, please say so, and I'll clarify what I mean.

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. All I can say is that by the decree of the presidency of the Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that decision was of 1992, two components of the armoured forces were established, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croat Defence Council. So that is the foundation for the establishment of the complete (sic), and the rest of the structure for both components of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, if there were two military forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina recognised by the central government in Sarajevo, why were you not appointed by the government in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the -- I take it that the courts of Bosnia-Herzegovina were based on the constitutional foundation of the republic itself, of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so it was the constitution which had been carried on over for some time. And that was the constitutional foundation of the Bosnia-Herzegovina courts?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there a constitutional foundation for the HVO or the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: You see, I am not an expert on constitutional law. I am a judge and I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I thought you might be able to help us with sort of tracing the legal source of your authority, that's all. I appreciate that you may not be expert in constitutional law, but I thought you may be able to help us with the legal source of your authority as a judge. That's all.

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: It is -- from the constitutional law point of view it was such a complex situation that, evidently, a more profound analysis of constitutional experts would be called for. And a judge cannot do that, because the situation was both legally and factually very complicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So if I posed a hypothetical situation. If a litigant was to appear before you and challenge your jurisdiction, what would you say to the litigant, in terms of your source of authority to be a judge and to be presiding over a case?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: We did not have such cases, anyone questioning the jurisdiction of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'll move on then. The investigative process. I think you were telling us yesterday that you were primarily interested and your jurisdiction was primarily concerned with activities by the HVO forces in terms of offences that they committed in relation to persons and property. Is that true? Is that a fair summary of what your jurisdiction was?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And your position was, in terms of the structure, you had the prosecutor and the HVO military police and yourself, and I take it that you were the most senior rank of those three positions?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why weren't you the most senior? You were the judge, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I occupied the senior position as regards the court, but not as regards the other two components, that is the military -- the military police and the prosecutor's office, which are completely independent of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Quite so. Yes. I'm sorry. Obviously, my question was confusing. When it came to the process of an investigation, when a matter required -- needed investigation, you would work co-operatively with the police and the prosecutor, but you would be in the most senior position of those in those circumstances, when you are exercising your jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I did not have any direct contact with the military police. It was the military prosecutor's office, and co-operation with the military police took place only on rare occasions, and it was only co-operation. There was no hierarchy there, because the military police was part of the structure of the military organisation of the Croat Defence Council as a component of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I take it what would happen is that you were the person that actually authorised the investigation? You were the one that made -- gave the approval to the investigation commencing?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it could be me or any other judge deciding that the request for an investigation submitted by the prosecutor contained enough elements, contained enough grounds for a reasonable -- that a particular person had committed a particular crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the prosecutor wouldn't be able to progress far through the system if he didn't obtain your approval for the investigation, because that was dependent -- because the investigation for it to continue through to an ultimate court case depended on you saying "I give my approval" in the form of a formal document?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So it's in that sense that I am saying that you were in a superior position to the prosecutor. You would agree with me there, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Only with regard to that particular segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the police, the police and the prosecutor dealt with each other, because he had -- the prosecutor had to obtain information and have crimes investigated, so the prosecutor would then, in turn, be superior to the police when it came to conducting an investigation. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Only when certain -- some preparative work was being proposed, but he was not -- the military police was not under the command or hierarchically subordinate to the judge. It was part of the military part of the Croat Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Of course. But if the -- but even if the commander of police wanted a case investigated and taken to court, he couldn't achieve that unless he had your authority, your approval?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So what he could -- he could conduct his own cases, could he?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: He can always submit a criminal report, and even without our consent, I mean the consent of the prosecutor and the court. In other words, when the military police responsible for crimes, when they decide that a particular crime has taken place, has been perpetrated, they can always submit a criminal report to the relevant prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the relevant prosecutor would then come to you, and you would authorise the investigation? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No. He would first turn -- he would first issue the request for investigation, which always -- which has a strict format and must contain so many specific elements, and then on the basis of its contents he must have reasonable grounds to suspect that an individual has committed a crime. And only in that case all the other proceedings follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I had taken that as said, that we'd go through all those steps first, but once you had done all of that, it would then come to you?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: What do you mean, they would come to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, to get authority, the approval to conduct the investigation. That's what you did, didn't you? You approved the commencement of investigations, once the reasonable suspicion had been established by the prosecutor; that was your job, part of your job?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: That request could not be proved without questioning of the suspect in the presence of his lawyer, and the prosecutor, only after that and in that case is it possible to reach a decision to open investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Let's assume that all of the formalities have been dealt with before it comes to you, and all of them are in place and in position. Once that's happened, once the prosecutor's done his job, you then authorise the formal investigation?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when it came to commencing an investigation, obviously the police are the most likely people to instigate the whole process right at the very beginning, once the crime is committed, and the reason why it's the police is because they are on the ground and close to the scene. So, generally speaking, it was the police that commenced the investigation. But was it possible for other parties to commence investigations?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No one could submit a request to commence investigation except for the authorised, the relevant prosecutor. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: -- according to the law in criminal procedure, the criminal report can be submitted by any citizen, not only the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when that is submitted by any citizen it goes to the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, does the prosecutor have a responsibility to then inform you?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So the prosecutor could just take it upon himself to ignore all these requests and choose not to investigate anything, if he wanted to?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, if the prosecutor did ignore everything and choose not to investigate crimes, you would be in a position to question the prosecutor as to why he was doing that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Either formally or informally?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Informally one could always have a discussion, but it was not necessary officially, in official terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And informally, if you had said to the prosecutor, "Don't you think that this matter should be investigated," it's likely you would have achieved some results, isn't it, having regard to your position?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Informally, as I said, yes, but not formally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It's interesting that Mr. Aleksovski actually contacted you, as well as the police and the prosecutor, when it came to the reporting of the murders that took place in February.

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So people could go to you directly?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify something. The situation was quite specific at the time. It was not something common or ordinary, and it was not a formal, it was not an official contact. It was of an informal nature. Mr. Aleksovski is a sociologist by profession. He is not a lawyer. He requested, informally, that I give him my opinion about that issue, that is, he asked me whether he had undertaken everything that was required in accordance with the law criminal procedure. He did that because he's not a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you gave him advice as to what he should do and, in fact, when you spoke to him, you were satisfied that he had done all that was necessary?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, indeed, any other person in an official position could have done a similar thing, couldn't they have?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I think that you said that at the time you made the comment that it was necessary for this matter to be expedited. Do you remember saying that in your evidence, or to be dealt with as quickly as possible?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, presumably, you could have, informally, taken steps to see that that happened? You had the position and authority to do it, maybe informally, but you could have said to the prosecutor, "I want this case dealt with quickly?"

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now I just want to clarify, if I could, the extent of the jurisdiction that you had. Now you dealt with crimes committed by HVO soldiers and you, I take it, didn't deal with crimes committed by soldiers of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina because that fell under the jurisdiction of the other court, is that true? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the sorts of crimes that you dealt with, were any crimes committed, but primarily with those connected with military personnel?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I take it that crimes committed by civilians didn't come under your jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Within the ten municipalities over which you had authority, it was any HVO forces within those ten municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I take it your jurisdiction would have related to such matters as murder, rape, destruction of property?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And these are the matters to which you and the prosecutor and the HVO police directed their attention, was it?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the military prison at Kaonik, which Mr. Aleksovski was the commander of came under your jurisdiction because of the fact that ultimately the court had a direct relationship to the prison? Is that right? Is that a fair assessment of it?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No. I only had supervision over the detained persons who were placed in that prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So if it came to construction works or the supplying of food or electricity or things of that nature, you had nothing to do with that?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What you were concerned with was the basis upon which the people were detained, the conditions under which they were detained and matters pertaining to prisoners and the legal rights of prisoners as such?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And that prison facility at Kaonik was exclusively devoted to people falling under the military structure, the military district?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was its purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do I take it from that at the same time concurrent with the Kaonik facility, civilian prisons in other places, perhaps, where people dealt with by the civilian courts were kept in custody?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know that and I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, if a case was brought before you and you looked at it and said, there is no connection with the HVO, it's just a crime, theft between two civilian parties, you wouldn't know where to send those people? You wouldn't try them yourself, but you wouldn't know where they're to go at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I didn't have such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So the filtering process was sufficiently accurate enough as to filter out any cases that were investigated by civilian police?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I only had supervision of detained military personnel. And yesterday I told you when it was that I went there. Again, I only had supervision against detained military personnel. That was my responsibility, my competence as regards what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, but the, you would agree with me, wouldn't you, from what you've said that the Kaonik facility was only built, and so far as the laws were concerned, related only to persons connected with or associated with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, are you suggesting to me that some other court or some other civilian investigation could put people in the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but when I was there, I told you I went there on several occasions, I only saw military personnel, members of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: With your understanding of what the facility was there for and its legal foundation?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you know of no other law which provided that this facility could be used for civilians or people who had committed crimes in the non-military structure, if I can call it that?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And in respect of the prison at Kaonik and its commander, in relation to your jurisdiction, you had supervisory authority over the commander of that facility, Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I did not have any jurisdiction over him. I had only supervisory role over the detained persons, detained individuals there. I did not have any such authority over the warden, that is Mr. Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you were responsible for their treatment, their hygiene and other conditions in detention?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No. No, I was not responsible for that. I only performed my supervisory role over these individuals. In case such an individual would state that the treatment was inadequate, I could only draw the attention of the warden to that fact. I did not have any supervision over Mr. Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, I'll read something that you said yesterday in your evidence. And you tell me with whether you now agree with it or disagree with it, if you might. It's 940, Your Honours, I have the rough transcript of it. Mr. Mikulicic asked you the question: "You said you only had supervisory function, what does it mean supervisory function over the detention unit." And you answered as follows: "Well, supervision over the detention unit by the criminal proceedings law of the Bosnia-Herzegovina, meant that after Bosnia-Herzegovina separated from Yugoslavia, you may put it that way, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted a decree, and took over the criminal proceedings act, which was formerly also the federal criminal proceedings act and as such was also in force in Bosnia-Herzegovina." And then you say and this is the significant part, I think: "One of its provisions said that a presiding judge also conducted supervision over detainees while they were kept under detention, but it meant what it meant is that their stay there, their treatment, hygiene and all other conditions in detention, for the duration of their detention." Didn't you say that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but we're talking about the supervision of detained individuals, not over the prison as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It's a fine point, isn't it, if they're being kept in conditions which aren't hygienic, or they're not receiving appropriate or satisfactory treatment, the jurisdiction may relate to the individuals, but surely if you have supervision, you would have authority to correct any irregularities that you found?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that authority lies only with the warden of the prison in cooperation with the relevant ministry, which organisationally speaking was linked to that particular prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you're completely without any authority. If you went out there and discovered a prisoner was living in squalor, and unhealthy conditions, was beaten all the time and you came to the conclusion that this was just totally unacceptable, you couldn't do anything about it, notwithstanding the fact it was your responsibility to supervise this?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't have such cases in respect of detained persons. If such a case would have occurred, I would have informed the warden and the relevant ministry with its seat in Mostar, that is the ministry of justice, who was in charge of undertaking all other necessary measures, if necessary, if it was necessary to rectify the situation. It is not, therefore, true that nothing could be undertaken. This was all regulated by law. By law that you have mentioned, by the law that you have mentioned and...

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did that law apply to you in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Which law did you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You called it the criminal proceedings law of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that's how you titled it.

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was a federal law, which was adopted by Bosnia-Herzegovina after it separated from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, which government of Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted it? The government in Mostar or the government in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: It was adopted by both governments, both governments adopted that law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you saw that law, did you, the adoption of that law by the government in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would it be correct to actually call it, I mean this is a small point, but would it be correct to call it the criminal law of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: It's the law on criminal procedure of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Wouldn't you call it the law on criminal procedure of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: That law was the law of criminal procedure of Bosnia-Herzegovina and also the law in criminal procedure of Herceg-Bosna, it was the same law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Getting back to the point we discussed a moment ago. You said that you couldn't give Mr. Aleksovski any directions, is that the effect of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No orders, except for orders that were prescribed by law. This could have been an order to bring a suspect for questioning, an order for transfer to another prison facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now what law prescribed that?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: The law on criminal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And that's not the law on criminal procedure of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I told you, it was one and the same law that was applicable throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, it certainly wouldn't have been adopted by the government in Sarajevo, it was part of the old federal law, wasn't it, and you wouldn't call it the law of Yugoslavia, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: This was a decree whereby the law on criminal procedure of the SFR was adopted. At the moment it was adopted, it became a law on, the law on criminal procedure of the newly established state, the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the status of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well you spoke of the newly established state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was just interested and curious about what you would call the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Do you want to hear my personal opinion or my opinion as a professional?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Either. Either one may assist us or both.

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I told you some time ago that the situation, constitutionally speaking, was such that Bosnia-Herzegovina, that situation requires analysis by an expert in constitutional law, I am afraid I couldn't help you here as a witness in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I thought you were going to give us your personal opinion, or is that your personal opinion?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I have given you my view and I do not wish to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the order that was put into evidence yesterday, Exhibit D-21/A you may want to look at it, if you would. And Mr. Registrar, if you would be so kind to give the witness also D-21/B. Now Mr. Percinlic, I want you, looking first at D-21/A, which is displayed on the screen. There's one thing I think we need to clear up straight away. In the English translation that I have, the last paragraph above your signature, describes Mr. Aleksovski as the commander of the district military court, I am not sure if that's a translation or typographical error, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: District military prison. Court assignment, no it means court or tribunal and this here word means prison. Prison, not court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I just need to clarify that. It's probably in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know what court means, here it should be prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you notice that Mr. Aleksovski has a fix affixed a stamp to that particular, I'm sorry you have affixed a stamp to that particular document, notice the stamp there?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And can you tell me what that stamp stands for, what it relates to?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: This is the stamp of the district military court in Travnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And who issued that stamp for your use?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: All courts were issued stamps from the relevant ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And so ministry of justice issued your stamp?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any connection between the ministry of justice and the ministry of defence?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And so the two particular departments of government as it were, functioned independently of each other, did they?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Well, I was not on the staff of the government in Mostar, so I do not know how they operated in practice or how they operated legally. I just don't know that, and especially I don't know how they acted in practice because that was in Mostar, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Would you look now for a moment at the next document, Exhibit 21/B. Now that document purports to be signed by Mr. Aleksovski, and there's also a stamp affixed to that, is there not?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It, the stamp has the words Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, central Bosnia, Central Bosnia operative zone, Travnic defence department, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you are not correct, it says the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and after that, the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna and you said the Croat republic of Herceg-Bosna, and then the Croatian community.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What I am interested is the Central Bosnia operative zone, Travnic defence department, what was the Central Bosnia operative zone?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I am not an expert on military matters, so I cannot tell you what operative zone means. All I can assume is that this is a kind of organisational unit of the armed forces, but I don't know what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I take it that like your stamp, this is a stamp that would have been issued to Mr. Aleksovski, presumably by the department of defence?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I do not know who he received it from, I know only from whom I received my stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now when it came to being given stamps, like the one you received, was there any formal procedure, did someone, you have to sign for it or were there regulations as to when and how you were to use it, can you tell me that?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: There were provisions specifying the use of stamps, but I just don't know if they were adopted at this time. It is the same time when the stamps were issued or were they adopted subsequently, it's very difficult to ascertain if one doesn't have the official gazette here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But surely you must have known in what circumstances you would affix the stamp or the seal to documents, you must have known that. You wouldn't haven't of had to look up in a gazette every time, surely?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: You asked me if there were any regulations pertaining to this matter, and I am answering that, yes, there were, but I don't know when they were adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps my question was a little misleading. Can you assist me by telling me when it was, under which circumstances you chose to affix the stamp to the document?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: As regulated, as prescribed and there are provisions on the use of the stamp and the inscription there. As I said, there's regulations on the use of stamps, but I simply do not know whether they were adopted in early '92 or in the course of '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, when you came to affix the stamp to this particular document, Exhibit D-21/A, presumably you must have had a reason for affixing it there, and you must have done so according to that reason, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why did you choose to use the stamp on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Because we stamp every single document, no document may leave the court without a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the stamp gives it the official sign of authority and approval, does it?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I guess one could assume from that that the stamp affixed by Mr. Aleksovski would have a similar effect?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know, I assume so, I don't know I am talking about the document that was issued by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now looking at the other exhibit that was tendered, Exhibit 22/A, and 22/B, perhaps you might be given both those documents. Now this related, this related, I think to an incident that's described to have taken place on the 7th of February, 1993, is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And we've gone over the fact that Mr. Aleksovski had contacted you about it, what did he tell you about the incident itself?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: You see it was a long time ago, all I remember is that two Bosniaks had been killed in Busovaca. He did not tell about the circumstances, all he said was that they lost their lives and aware of the fact that at the same time, those undesirable events had taken place, I simply told him a what needed to be done. And he had already done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I take it that Mr. Aleksovski was concerned about it, because the victims were persons who were in his prison establishment?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: It is quite possible. I repeat, it was a long time ago, but Mr. Aleksovski had a high sense of responsibility and I didn't know that at the time. But I could see from the conversation with him that he was very worried about that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he tell you why he was worried about it?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: He didn't say that people were asking questions or anything of that nature? When I say people, I mean people from the international community, the Red Cross or BCMM or any of those organisations?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No. It was a very brief conversation on the telephone and one could not learn from it or judge by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you act on this matter yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: What matter? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This investigation, the one, the subject of Exhibits 22/A and B. Did you take action?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I remember that in the morning I spoke to the prosecutor who said -- who told me then that all the actions were taken in order to note down all the relevant facts about that crime and to bring in the detained -- the suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, to your knowledge, did all of that happen?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time all that was necessary was done to launch, to start the criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did the criminal proceedings go through to their ultimate conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know, because I left that post, I left the office, so I do not know when they were brought to a close. I mean, when the proceedings were brought to a close.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you leave -- sorry, when did you leave that post?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I left the post sometime in mid-1995, but I told you that during the military operations in Travnik in 1993 another relevant part of the court records stayed behind, in part in the court building, in part outside it. So that the reopening of these cases lasted throughout 1994 and in the beginning of 1995 and I remember, I personally remember, that I took part in the reopening of some of these cases. However, you have to realise that it was very difficult to reopen these cases because a large part of the documentation was destroyed during the military operations in one way or the other, in other words, burnt, seized or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann. Excuse me. Perhaps we might take a recess now, also to allow the witness to rest. Therefore, I propose a 20-minute recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Percinlic, we were talking about Exhibits 22/A and 22/B, which is the investigation into the incident that occurred on 7 February, 1993. You are saying you weren't sure what had happened to the case, and we were talking about the case being reconstructed. Did you ascertain what happened to the accused? They were taken into custody. I take it, they are not still there waiting for their trial?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I don't know. No. As far as I heard, one or two of them have died in the meantime, and here I am talking about the four individuals from the request to open investigation. Two individuals, as far as I know, have died in the meantime. Under what circumstances, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, the remaining two, were they ever tried, that you know of?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I don't know. As I told you, in April, May '95, I left that post and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I assume if they had been remanded in custody pending the trial or during the investigation phase, what would have happened, though, between 1993 and 1995, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: See, as I told you, this reconstruction of cases lasted for very long, a year and a half, due to some objective circumstances. You must bear in mind that war operations were conducted at the time in the area. However, all the cases have been reconstructed pursuant to an order to reconstruct a number of cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of that. But you had supervision of the prisoners? That was your responsibility. So, surely, even if there was a period when records may have been destroyed, you would have been concerned to inquire as to the fate of your prisoners, surely?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Indeed, did you go to the camp in March of 1993 for the purpose of seeing these particular prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I went there in late March, 1993. As far as I can recall, I saw them on that occasion. I couldn't give you the exact date, but I think it was either in March or in April. I didn't know these individuals personally and during that period a number of individuals were detained, so I cannot specifically recall these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, were all of the persons detained in the camp done so as a consequence of either orders by you, or your fellow judges?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I only saw such persons, that is the persons who were detained there. However, you must bear in mind that in 1993 there were also convicts there, as well as some members of the Croatian Defence Council because of disciplinary measures that were taken against them. I didn't see such cases because, in January, 1993, and in April, 1993, in Vitez and Busovaca respectively, I did not have any direct contact with the prison, because the seat of the court was in Travnik, and I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But notwithstanding the fact that you were physically separated from the prison, your responsibilities and duties of supervision still continued during that period?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, only in respect of detained persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you were able to make contact with the prison by means of telephone or fax machine during that time, even if you physically couldn't travel there?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: At the time of war operations that contact was also rare, and it was possible to establish such contact only from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, this document, 22/B -- 22/A and 22/B, obviously you would have read these documents because the persons incarcerated as a consequence of this investigation come under your supervision?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the reason why Mr. Aleksovski became involved in the matter was because they were persons, that people were victims to the crimes were persons who had been taken out of his prison facility, prison facility that he was responsible for. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I don't know how it happened, the incident in question, and I couldn't know that at the time. It was only after the request to open investigation was submitted that I learned how the incident came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The victims had been taken out for the purposes of trench digging, hadn't they? That's what you learned either at the time or later?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: That's what is stated in the request to open investigation, and I believed it to be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, indeed, in Exhibit 22/B, immediately under the heading, "because there are reasonable grounds to suspect that," and it sets out the day and a date and so forth, they say, "They killed Nermin Elezovic and Jasmin Sehovic, Muslims who had been taken prisoner by the HVO during the clashes between the HVO from Bosnia -- from Busovaca and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's the clash that took place in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you were aware that these people had been detained in the prison at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that. I told you I didn't have contact with the institution after mid January, 1993. However, I heard, I don't know exactly when, that there were persons who were detained there on that particular locality. However, I personally did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, were they -- were those persons that were detained there, those Muslim persons, detained under your authority?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, who else had authority to put people in the prison facility at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I was working for a civilian institution. I was therefore in the civilian part, civilian wing of the HVO, not the military one, so I don't know who within the military wing was responsible for that, had the authority for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you were in the district military court. Now, whether -- I am not suggesting you were a military officer.

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you were in a district military court, and its responsibility was for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it was under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice and not the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But it doesn't matter what ministry it was under, you told me that the prison facility at Kaonik was established for the purposes of dealing with persons connected with or associated with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were these Muslim prisoners doing there, then? They weren't connected or associated with the HVO, were they?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There is not a thing here to suggest that that's the case. And, indeed, if they had been connected with it or associated with the HVO, they would immediately come under your jurisdiction, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, if you saw persons exercising your jurisdiction, or reports such as this, which indicated that somebody else was exercising your jurisdiction, you would have done something about it, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, what did you do about it when you read this?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: What? You mean the request to open investigation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you found out that there were Muslim prisoners taken by the HVO, incarcerated in Kaonik, and then subsequently killed trench digging, what did you do about it?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: We conducted criminal proceedings. The prison was not under my jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you conduct criminal proceedings into why these Muslim prisoners were being incarcerated in the Kaonik Prison by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Because the request to open investigation didn't go in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It says that the criminal report was filed by the military police in Vitez. Was that the headquarters of the military police, or was there also military police in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: In Vitez it was the criminal police that had its seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's a translation error. You say in Vitez or Busovaca? Maybe there is a mistake there. Was it in Busovaca there was civilian police and in Vitez the military police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: The seat of the criminal military police was in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. So that's why the report was -- why the matter was investigated by those police --

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, were you aware that during 1992 there was published in the Narondi List, which is the gazette of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosnia, an agreement between the president of the HVO, Mate Boban, and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina a decree which determined that the Geneva Conventions would apply to enemy soldiers, in those days it was the JNA and other forces. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know. I read these -- the Official Gazette daily, but it's been -- it was a long time ago, and a number of them were issued, and it is hard to remember each detail and each particular decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand that from my own experience. So perhaps you might look at this document, if I can show it to you. There's a copy for Your Honours, and I've given a copy to Mr. Mikulicic. I understand we are short a copy. I'll do what I can, Your Honours. I think I've given two documents there, in any event. Perhaps they can both be marked for the moment. But it's the top document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be document 123.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As I just indicated, there is one attached to it. Perhaps that could be 123/B, if that's convenient to the Registrar. There are two documents in the list. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, just looking at the top document there, the decree on the treatment of persons captured. Do you note that, see that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Niemann. Is it possible to place the document on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By all means, Your Honours. I am wondering if you would assist me. Could the English version be put on the ELMO. And you can keep the Croatian version there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, just looking at this document for me. Do you recognise this as the typical Narondi List that was presented at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You will notice that, of course, the date of it is 3rd of July, 1992, and it relates at that stage to primarily the conflict with the JNA, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes. And at that time I did not read, I did not see this Narondi list issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You'll see there that it deals with persons captured in armed fighting against the Croatian community, et cetera, shall be treated in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. I think as a lawyer you would expect that to be the case anyway, would you not?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The second article, Article 2, provides that: "The head of justice and administration department --" I take it, that's your department, is it, the head of justice and administration department?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: "-- in co-operation with the head of the defence department, and the head of the department of the interior." And that's the police, I take it?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. "Shall designate the locations where prisoners shall be kept," which in this case, in the relevant case here, is Kaonik. Kaonik is not mentioned, of course, but they indicate where they shall be kept. "In accordance with the provisions of the convention."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you have an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My learned friend, Mr. Niemann, before he began to examine the witness, informed me about the document that he would show to the witness, and I did not react then, but now, when I see the thrust of the cross-examination, I feel I must object. My learned friend from the prosecutor's office showed the witness the decree on the treatment of persons captured in armed conflicts, that is, persons who could be defined as prisoners of war, and pursuant to the indictment the proceedings here are not conducted against persons who are captured in armed conflicts but against civilians. The Defence holds that this manner of examination of the witness, which pertains to prisoners of war, even if disregarding the fact that this is a period which is not covered by the indictment, is not relevant to these proceedings, and therefore we object against the cross-examination of the witness, which would be on the treatment of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, what is the relevance that led you to make this objection? Do you understand my question? I'm sorry, let me repeat it. Perhaps I was not clear. You stated that you took cognizance of this document; is that correct? Did you know this document before it was presented to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I saw this document today, right before the trial when Mr. Niemann showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You only saw the document, but you did not know how it would be used by the Prosecution; is that it? What did you think that the Prosecution was going to do with this document? You didn't know?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really did not know what was the intent behind this form of examination of my learned friend. I may have thought that my learned friend simply wanted to show a document which was an official organ at the time, but I did not know what would be the thrust of his examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, can you state what is your objective in the use of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honours, the significance of international law of a -- I call it quasi-state, because I don't think we know what the community of Herceg-Bosnia is, actually, but it does have its own army and it seems to have its own territory, which are some things consistent with a state. It's very significant when a state, or such an institution, expresses itself to be bound by the Geneva Conventions. And, in my submission, the document is shown to the witness for a number of reasons. Firstly, for that fact, which is a very relevant fact. It doesn't matter that a state says, well, we accept that we are bound by the Geneva Conventions for this conflict. It doesn't assist for someone to come along and say, "Oh it wasn't this conflict, it was this conflict over here." Once one expresses themselves bound by the conventions, they are bound by the conventions. So that's the first point that I wish to make. The second point is that it's all been a bit mysterious about this relationship of the Department of Justice in this community and the Department of Defence. This document seems to deal with that issue, and deals with it in Article 2. And, ultimately, the document clearly expresses the position with respect to the facility at Kaonik in Article 3, and under whose jurisdiction it comes. And because this witness is a person who was appointed to the district military court, has said that he is responsible for offences perpetrated by HVO or connected with HVO, in my respectful submission it becomes very relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, what is your position, after having heard what Mr. Niemann stated?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence wishes to indicate the title of the document, which is used by the Prosecution. It is a decree on the treatment of persons captured in armoured conflicts, fighting, that is persons enjoying the status of prisoners of war and therefore are under Geneva Conventions. And I am repeating this particular case has nothing to do with prisoners of war. This case is dealing with civilians rather than the prisoners of war. And that is why we object against the use of this document and any examination of it in this direction. We have yet another objection, and that is that my learned friend is examining the witness as concerns the constitutional law aspects, whereas at that time the witness was the criminal judge of the district military court in Travnik. So that was his duty. And our examination of the same witness was within this framework.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And, Mr. Mikulicic, what do you feel about the clarification about the administrative structure which was raised by the Article 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we still hold that this document is of no relevance in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I will now consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before you consult, may I just raise one -- correct one matter, I think. We've never asserted that the indictment only deals with civilians. Admittedly, most of the evidence points to that, but we've never asserted that that's the position under the indictment. So it may be that that's the way the evidence comes out at the end of the day, but it's not our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The decision of the Chamber, for the time being, is that we will take a ten-minute break. I believe that ten minutes will be sufficient for Mr. Aleksovski to be able to leave the courtroom; is that right? Very well, ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 11.55 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic and Mr. Niemann, the Chamber has considered that the date of the document is not relevant because we consider that the document was in effect at the time of the indictment. Therefore, the Chamber will admit the document only in the case of Article 2 which is in question concerning the structure and organisation of the state. This is the principle that was admitted at the beginning of his testimony. So, Mr. Niemann, you may continue with the cross-examination within the area of Article 2 only of this document. This is the decision of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Looking at Article 2, Mr. Percinlic, you will agree with me there that it is expressly stated that there shall be cooperations between those three departments when it comes to the dealing with prisoners, in this case, prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And it's true, isn't it, that a similar regime operated in 1993 as well as in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when the district military prosecutor's office was established, there were four districts established, I think that's right, isn't it? One in Mostar, Duvno, Travnik and Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes there were three established.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think I said four, I said Mostar, Duvno Travnik and Bosanski Brod, does that sound right to you?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes. I believe that three were established. I don't have that decree. Yes, you're right, four.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the prosecutor was commissioned with the responsibility of acting upon complaints that were afforded to him by military personnel, and I think as you said in evidence, citizens, military commanders and institutions could all refer matters to the military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Criminal reports could be submitted by any citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And members of the armed forces and also commanders, you'd agree, I think, with that?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Aleksovski, of course, was a member of such an institution and we've already discussed the investigation that was referred to you -- referred, sorry, to the military prosecutor and that he'd discussed with you. Did he discuss with you any other incidences at the time that troubled him, such as the treatment of Muslim inmates in the prison?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No, no, this did not fall within my jurisdiction and I never discussed this with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, if they had been put in there by the HVO, that would be an act that would certainly fall within your jurisdiction, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No, because no criminal report was submitted against these persons. There was no investigation against them and they were not under my jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But when the Muslim detainees were murdered and Mr. Aleksovski contacted you, you had no report then either, did you? This was pre the submission of any report or prior to?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: On that occasion I just gave him my advice and recommendation. It was an informal contact. It was not a formal, official contact as it is prescribed by law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But he certainly could have contacted you if he was concerned about the treatment of prisoners, the fact that they were being taken out and used for trench digging or for human shields or some such thing. He could have raised that with you?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No, he couldn't discuss this with me because I was not the person in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You're saying officially he may not have been able to do it, but surely he could do it if he wanted to, you're in contact with him, you're speaking to him on the phone, he could have said to you, I am concerned about this issue, couldn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: He could say so, but he never did. Again, as I told you, this contact was rather rare. There were military operations going on in the territory of Busovaca and Vitez municipalities and our contacts were rare and official in character.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you could have given him advice if he had raised that, he said to you; "I have people here that have been placed in my prison and they're being taken out each day and used as human shields or to dig trenches, and that worries me and concerns me, I think it might be contrary to the Geneva conventions," he could have raised that and you could have given him advice, couldn't you, based on what he should do?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what advice would you have given him if you'd done that?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Again, I have to reiterate that this was not under my jurisdiction, that it was under the jurisdiction of military, of the military wing, that is the army. The military court was not competent for giving any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Sorry, to interrupt you, but I believe Mr. Mikulicic would like to raise an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with all due respect for the line of questioning of my learned colleague we do have an objection because the prosecutor has been asking hypothetical questions to this witness. What would have happened if you had done this or that. I mean, this is a very hypothetical and the witness cannot provide any facts. He can only base his conclusions on the basis of some speculation and this is what we object to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There's no fundamental objection to asking a hypothetical question, provided they're based in some sense of reality and I think that's certainly the case here. We have a very clearly defined situation by the witness that if he becomes involved in an investigation, the prisoners under his responsibility or under his supervision, they're all clearly defined, yet we know from the evidence that there are hundreds of people kept in this prison and there is no foundation about it at all. Surely I am entitled to explore that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: It was stated and we should be reminded of two things: First of all, that the witness is not an expert witness. The second thing is that we admitted that we could clarify issues concerning the organisation. In any event, I believe we should stick to the facts. If a hypothesis can clarify these facts but not in abstract terms. Do you agree with this point? We could, we might put questions in a conditional sense as long as these will be an aid to clarifying certain facts, but not in abstract terms. If you accept this point, then we will then move ahead, if you do not, then we'll make a decision on this issue. Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'll word it another way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went to the Kaonik facility on the number of occasions that you did so during, did you see Muslim detainees there?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And other than going to the place where the cells were, did you go anywhere else in the facility?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It was a notorious fact, wasn't it, that Muslim facilities were being kept in this camp, in this prison facility, you knew that?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: This is what I heard after the first conflict. I heard that there were such persons. But, again, I must tell you that I did not have the opportunity to -- did not have physical access to these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well now, if an HVO soldier breached the Geneva conventions, that would be a matter that would concern you, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: Yes, in case a criminal report is submitted, in case proceedings are conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Of course that you formerly became involved in the matter, but you'd be concerned about matters that breached the Geneva convention, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: In case criminal proceedings are initiated as it is regulated by law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you suggesting to me that most criminal proceedings initiated either in your capacity as a judge or in any other capacity, you had no interest in breaches of the law, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZELKO PERCINLIC
utterances.text: I did not say that. I simply told you how the proceedings were conducted and what principle was applied. But I think that you keep mixing the role of the prosecutor's office and the role of the court in this type of proceedings. It was not the court that initiated proceedings, it was the responsibility of the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I know, but we covered that very clearly. But the point of the fact is that if you were travelling around the is district and you see, saw or heard of, or become aware of breaches of the Geneva conventions and other crimes being committed on a regular basis by HVO soldiers, if you're receiving no reports of that, that would be a matter of concern to you, wouldn't it?
